#307. Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

A new project and exhibition, "The Night Watch Lives," lifts the veil on the hidden world of microbes covering one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.

Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius."

In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.

Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.

The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?

The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention."

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch."

Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.

These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.

At the exhibition's opening on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the coming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.

That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us."

People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," says van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013.  How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery."

The samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again."

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.

As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch.'"

The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.

And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project."

The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

#304. Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth

Spreading alkaline rock on fields to lock away carbon helps farmers at first, but new research shows that those benefits could be strictly limited.

Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.

But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”

The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.

Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and  academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.

The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.

“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”

Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post. She also criticized the nonprofit for not contacting the company before posting its results and for publishing them on a blog instead of in peer-reviewed literature.Kukla says CarbonPlan did account for higher applications of crushed rock in its analysis.

A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.

But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the company accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”

Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

Yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the new findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.

Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s important to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.

“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.

These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.

New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid.

Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

#302. The Best TVs We’ve Tested (2026): Samsung, LG, TCL, Sony, and More.

Buying a new TV is always a big decision, namely because its a big piece of tech with a permanent place in your home that you'll be staring at for hours on end. Not to mention, some of the best of the best cost thousands of dollars. It doesn't help that most TVs look exactly the same and have nondescript names like the Samsung S95H—not great for narrowing your options.

Fear not. After stress-testing multiple TVs this year, I can attest to one simple truth: in 2026, you have more great options than ever. Art TVs and RGB TVs exploded onto the market and made the typical “just buy an OLED TV” advice seem like an ancient relic of a bygone. These top-performing televisions are my “desert island” picks, if said island had a power generator and good popcorn.

For more audio and home theater recommendations, check out related guides to the best OLED TVs, the best art TVs, the best RGB TVs, the best home theater projectors, and the best soundbars. If you truly don't know where to start, try our guide on how to buy a TV.

Update November 2026: We've revamped this entire guide, replacing nearly all of our top picks, Honorable Mentions, and Other TVs We've Tested.

The great debate: which size television is best for your living room? Does it even matter? The first thing to consider is price: an 80-inch TV is going to cost significantly more than a 65-inch one. In some cases, that means an extra grand or two for the privilege of seeing the stubble on Spider-Man’s face in great detail. Broadly speaking, the larger the room, the more useful a large screen is. The most popular size is 65 inches, which is a great option for most medium sizes spaces.

I’m partial to art televisions for one simple reason: They are useful even when they are turned off. Art TVs use an antireflective layer on top of the screen to create more realistic, textured still images like artwork or paintings. The best ones can replace a picture frame or wall art in any room, and double as great TVs.

TV tech has evolved in 2026, and the new kid on the block is RGB TVs. These new models shine red, blue, and green light through an LCD panel to create brighter, more vibrant color. OLED on the other hand can control the color of individual pixels and even turn them off completely, leading to excellent contrast and black levels.

Which one performs the best? That depends. RGB models like the LG Micro RGB Evo provide more control over picture quality, brightness, and contrast. OLED televisions like the Samsung S95H tend to look better on movie night, especially for nighttime scenes when inky blacks need to look realistic. If pressed, I’d pick an RGB TV model because you get more control over color, but that's just me.

I picked Samsung's The Frame Pro (2026) as the best overall TV because it has stunningly good picture quality and looks incredible showcasing a masterpiece painting on your wall. I remember staring at the 65-inch model on the wall of my office for two months, just marveling at high-res shipwreck photos and the real wood bezels that encompass the screen (and snap easily into place, by the way). With just about every painting, The Frame Pro showed intricate and detailed textures, as though you could reach out and feel the waves of an ocean or curve of a face.

The Frame Pro is also an excellent choice for movies and shows. Because of the anti-glare screen and matte finish, the dark corridors of scenes in The Batman on HBO had extra depth and animated movies like Toy Story 5 on Disney+ popped with color. Sure, it doesn't have the true black pixels of an OLED screen, but its other capabilities more than make up for it.

Extra features included easy-to-install stands (no screws needed) and a breakout box called the Samsung Wireless One Connect that lets you connect streaming devices and a game console from across the room. That means fewer wires dangling on the wall.

TCL is a more budget-focused television maker that tends to undercut the price of brands like Samsung and LG. A good example of this is the TCL QM7L Mini-LED TV above, which has a budget-friendly price but anything but oriented picture quality. If anything, this QLED model competes with some OLED TVs for inky, deep blacks and rich color. Will you notice any contrast issues when you watch the latest Pixar film? Probably not, especially since the QM7L also looked exceptionally bright in our tests.

A few other extras to mention: We loved the backlit remote, which makes it easier to punch up the volume or adjust picture quality settings in a dark room. You might even be able to skip a soundbar with this TV—the internal Bang & Olufsen speakers sound nice and loud.

Samsung, TCL, Hisense, and Sony released new RGB TVs this year, but it's the LG Micro RGB Evo that takes the crown, namely because you can tweak so many of its picture settings. In my tests,I could tweak the picture so much that movies and shows that mostly take place at night still looked visible, clear, and realistic. As one example among many, I remember tweaking settings for the movie Awake, a largely dark film, to the point where it looked clear and colorful. Other RGB models from Hisense and even Samsung struggled with those same dark scenes, no matter which setting I used.

Another major plus is that this model supports 100 percent of the color gamut specs for BT.2020, DCI-P3, and Adobe RGB. In layman's terms, if you watch a movie like Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (which also matches those specs), you will see a true rainbow of every color available, with unmatched color vibrancy. This TV is so striking that I came away thinking that OLED TVs are no longer the obvious gold standard in 2026.

Samsung made a big change to their flagship OLED model this year, the Samsung S95H. They ditch the Samsung One Connect breakout box that was required with previous models (and is still required on TVs like The Frame Pro). The TV now has ports directly on the panel, where you can connect video game consoles, streaming devices, or Blu-ray players directly. While that might create more cable clutter, I found it much easier to use than the previous Samsung S95F.

Perhaps more importantly, the S95H is a top performer when it comes to picture quality and settings. I could adjust the contrast and brightness to perfectly light famously dim shows like Game of Thrones. As an OLED, the blacks look richer and darker, more so than most RGB models. The AI optimization picture settings here are actually useful—during soccer matches, the TV adjust to make the pitch look even greener and minimizes background crowd noise, for example.

It's a bit pricey, but the overall brightness, contrast, color quality, and even built-in sound are all premium-grade.

The company famous for streaming sticks released its first OLED TV this year, and it follows the brand's formula of low-cost simplicity. Roku has, up until this point, stuck with LED TV models with average performance. Wonder of wonders, the Pro Series is not bad at all, making even dark scenes in movies like Solo: A Star Wars Story look vibrant and colorful. Outside of picture quality, Roku makes things as easy as possible, with features like Smart Picture Max, which automatically tweaks picture settings for you, a simple TV operating system (Roku OS, of course), and an uncluttered remote.

I will say, the brightness and contrast are good for this price, but nowhere near the cinema-quality color of something like the premium Samsung S95H. I think it's a great option for anyone on a budget or for people who only watch TV occasionally.

The Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) is my TV of the year, but the Amazon Ember Artline is also a capable, significantly cheaper, art TV. Just don't expert as premium of an image in movies and TV shows.

Art televisions use a matte finish on the screen to help make paintings look more realistic and textured. The Ember Artline achieves this look, and even includes frame bezel that snap into place around the screen (these are sold separately on Samsung's Frame TVs). I loved looking at painting on this TV, including some animated ones Amazon offers in the catalog. Using the TV is simple, and the improved Alexa+ voice assistant is useful for changing the volume (hands free) or finding obscure sci-fi films.

Image quality isn't the big selling point of this TV: the art, aesthetic, and low price are. Gamers will find the 60 Hz refresh rate lacking, especially for twitchy action titles. Contrast and brightness are okay, but not nearly as impressive as something like the Samsung The Frame Pro. But keep in mind: this TV is far, far cheaper than premium options.

While the LG Micro RGB Evo is endlessly tweakable and outperformed every other RGB model I tested for picture quality, the Sony BRAVIA 9 II RGB TV still takes the cake when it comes to gaming. That’s especially true if you own a Sony PlayStation 5, since the TV will automatically adjust the picture quality and latency to match the game console. I tested it mostly using a high-end PC, and at a 120 Hz refresh rate, latency felt non-existent to me.

I also found this TV to be a capable alternative to a premium OLED. Red, green, and blue colors are almost infinitely adjustable. During a scene in Toy Story 5 by a tree in a field, the sun creates splashes of color that look incredibly lush and vivid. Watching Game of Thrones, I found I could enable a special black level setting to make night battles look more realistic.

The Bravia 9 II uses Google TV OS and Google Gemini voice assistant, which both run simply, smoothly, and with no weird hiccups. While the LG Micro RGB Evo is a better performer for color and contrast, the BRAVIA 9 II’s gaming features, fast performance, high-end speakers, and deep blacks are exceptional.

Hisense UR9 RGB Mini-LED: My top pick for a midrange RGB, the Hisense UR9 has rich colors thanks to RGB tech shining red, green, and blue pixels. Some scenes, including ones in the movie The Last Duel, looked extra crisp and colorful. But it's not quite as excellent as my top picks.

LG B6 OLED: The LG B6 is a great budget-friendly OLED TV that performed very similarly to the Roku Pro Series OLED. Either one of them would serve you well, but we gave the nod to the Roku TV for it's lower price, simpler remote, and easy to use Roku operating system.

Samsung Micro RGB R95H: Samsung's Micro RGB display tech didn’t make the Samsung Micro RGB R95H stand out from the competition as much as I'd hoped. In fact, the LG Micro RGB Evo responded much better to picture quality adjustments, and while shows and movies looked colorful and clear, they weren't quite as jaw-dropping as similarly priced RGB and OLED competitors.

Sony Bravia 7 II: The Sony Bravia 7 II is unfortunately outclassed by the other midrange RGB TV on this list: the Hisense UR9. It is more expensive, it's harder to set up, and the picture quality doesn't quite match that of the Hisense TV.

Sony Bravia 8 II: Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata tested this stunning high-end OLED, and praised it's top-notch image quality and processing. That said, the Samsung S95H is newer, about the same price, and has a more striking, glare-free image than the Sony Bravia 8 II.

TCL Nxtvision Series Art: This budget art TV simply cannot compete with similarly low-priced art TVs like the Amazon Ember Artline TV and Hisense Class S7 CanvasTV. Both offer better picture quality and a better general user experience. You can read my full review here.

TCL RM9L RGB Mini-LED: The TCL RM9L RGB TV is huge and hugely expensive. The $6,000 85-inch is the smallest and cheapest model you can get, and it is generally outclassed by the LG Micro RGB Evo.

The WIRED reviews team is busy testing the ever-popular midrange LG C6 and premium LG G6. Given past performances from LG C and G-series TVs, we expect them to be strong contenders for top accolades in this guide.

#301. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

#300. Blade Runner 2099 finally takes this franchise to the stars

Blade Runner 2099 walks lovingly in the footsteps of Ridley Scott and Denis Villeneuve's preceding Blade Runner films, echoing their memorable cyberpunk settings and noir detective stories. However, there's one area where the TV show completely outpaces both films.

Like Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049, Blade Runner 2099 takes place primarily in Los Angeles, rarely leaving the city outskirts. Its world is one of bustling streets, crowded apartment buildings, and the massive pyramids that tower over the Los Angeles skyline. Yet episode 2 opens with a different landscape entirely: a fiery red terrain bursting with rocky crags and rushing lava flows.

This is Namaka Moon, a real-life satellite of the dwarf planet Haumea. It's also the first time an on-screen Blade Runner project has been to space. (Notably, comic Blade Runner 2019: Off World has already blasted off to space.)

Space travel is a fact of life in the world of Blade Runner, as well as in its source material, Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? As part of larger space colonization attempts, humans are moving to off-world settlements. Who is preparing these settlements for human occupation? Replicants (or androids in the novel), whose enhanced strength and durability make them the ideal slave labor force for braving inhospitable outer space environments.

While off-world colonies seem prime for sci-fi exploration, they have just been a background world-building detail in the Blade Runner franchise. Billboards frequently tease the promise of a new off-world home, while extraterrestrial landmarks like Orion take center stage in Roy Batty's (Rutger Hauer) iconic "tears in rain" monologue. Neither the Blade Runner films nor the animated series Blade Runner: Black Lotus have ever left Earth.

That all changes with Blade Runner 2099's Namaka Moon opening. The sequence focuses not on what life in an off-world colony looks like, but rather the labor that goes into establishing one in the first place.

In the episode, replicant Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) clambers across the moon's rocky surface, establishing a series of beacons that shoot beams of light into Namaka's cloudy atmosphere. Once she leaves the moon, the beacons detonate in a series of spectacular explosions, presumably the first step in Namaka's terraforming process. As she tells companion replicant Marek (Johnny Harris), Namaka will be ready for human habitation in 20 years' time thanks to her work. Fittingly, the episode is titled "Birther of Worlds."

The Namaka sequence does a spectacular job of ushering Blade Runner into its own Space Age. But it isn't just a trip to space for space's sake. The entire episode opening is rooted in the replicant experience: the loneliness of traversing a perilous moon alone. The awe of watching a world come to life thanks to your handiwork. The hollowness of realizing you will never live in that world, nor be recognized for that work. It's key to understanding Olwen's character, as well as understanding the role of replicants in general. You could almost imagine Roy performing a similar task back in his day.

Plus, since Blade Runner 2099 has yet to show what an actual off-world colony might look like, it still leaves the door open for future Blade Runner projects to flesh out that aspect of the world onscreen. Clearly, the world is far, far vaster than just Los Angeles. Maybe Namaka is just the beginning.

#298. Budget cuts threaten Germany's fight against antisemitism and racism

Numerous grassroots initiatives in Germany are facing funding cuts. Affected organizations are sounding the alarm, pointing to growing challenges posed by far-right extremism.

Initiatives and organizations in Germany are speaking out against planned budget cuts to the work of strengthening democracy and fighting racism and antisemitism. Berlin is planning drastic savings measures in its draft federal budget for 2027, which is to be debated in parliament this Friday.

The "Living democracy" (Demokratie Leben) program from the Ministry for Family Affairs is set to receive a total of €170 million ($187 million). That is about €20 million less than the current year's budget allocation.

The draft was agreed upon by Germany's governing coalition of the conservative Union – of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) – and the center-left Social Democrats.

Numerous organizations consider the cuts a dire signal. Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, a Berlin-based NGO which campaigns against right-wing extremism and discrimination, sees many initiatives in Germany under existential threat.

"In view of the antisemitic agitation, the open violence and the ever-increasing legitimization of its normalization, it is concerning that the very structures and grants which do something to oppose them are now standing on the verge of collapse," Ameer explained during a media briefing alongside other like-minded organizations.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to the initiatives, the work to strengthen democratic civil society could suffer lasting damage, because long-established structures cannot simply be rebuilt after they have been destroyed.

The thing that outraged many organizations: The cuts come at a time when the extreme right is celebrating numerous election victories in Germany.

The  Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are considered far-right extremist, achieved record-high results in several elections in 2026, most notably in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. "Especially in view of the AfD possibly coming into government in Saxony-Anhalt, we need these structures more urgently than ever," urged Tahera Ameer.

The promotion of democratic civil society in Germany has been controversial for years. While initiatives and associations regularly appeal for more money, some conservative politicians repeatedly criticize an alleged one-sidedness in the allocation of public funds.

During the federal parliamentary debate on the funding program in March 2025, Christian Democrat politician Marvin Schulz supported the planned changes, which were put forward by German Families Minister Karin Prien, also of the CDU: "We need new areas of focus," he said. Projects working against extreme Islamism and antisemitism were underrepresented, he said.

But initiatives to combat antisemitism will also receive less funding in the future. The Central Committee of German Catholics (ZdK) criticized cuts to the Federal Association of Departments for Research and Information on Antisemitism (RIAS), the nationwide OFEK counselling center for people affected by antisemitic violence and discrimination, and the German Alliance against Islamophobia and discrimination against Muslims, (CLAIM).

The ZdK called on the German government to continue its advocacy for the protection of Jewish and Muslim life and secure this structurally and financially. They say planned cuts achieve the opposite and are a fatal signal to a diverse and democratic society.

The AfD went further in its criticism: The party called for the funding to be stopped entirely, calling the initiatives a "program for the Left to secure power for itself."

If the AfD governs in Saxony-Anhalt, it wants wide-ranging cuts. The party wants to completely abolish the renowned State Center for Civic Education and cut state funding from numerous other organizations.

In December, the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, wants its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund to be the first AfD state premier to head a state government.

A spokesperson from the federal government's Family Affairs Ministry responded to questions from DW by referring to the need for the government to consolidate its budget. The goal was that funding programs "reliably continue, also in 2027, and make the biggest and widest impact possible with the means available."

However, an alliance of several organizations does not want to give up and is calling for a complete reversal of the decision: Instead of implementing the cuts, the organizations want the government to boost the funding pool by €50 million.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Work to strengthen democracy must be funded," urged Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation. "That is a priority that we are currently not seeing. And that is very unsettling."

Many organizations point out that the consequences of the cuts will not remain abstract. They will have very real effects on people who experience discrimination in Germany, Lina Mitschke fears. She leads the Berlin association "Each One Teach One" (EOTO), an education and empowerment organization for people of color.

"The needs haven't gone away. But from January, people coming in have nobody to properly speak with; the phone will no longer be picked up; emails will go unanswered if someone needs support," she said.

For organizations such as EOTO, the planned cuts are a bitter setback. In past years, they had managed to raise awareness of the lived reality of Black people in Germany. "The experiences of more than a million Black people in Germany would be negated with the cuts," Mitschke said.

The associations want to fight until the very end to reverse the decision. They say work to promote and support democracy is what holds society together.

#297. A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

Anthropic warned investors that AI might be conscious—but acting accordingly could hurt its business. So what’s the plan?

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models' production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.

Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

#296. Blade Runner 2099 sneaks in a book detail that never made it into the movies

As adaptations go, Blade Runner is a fairly loose take on Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?

The 1982 film replaces the novel's androids (or "andys") with replicants. Characters from the novel were cut, including Iran, the wife of Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford), and John Isidore, who houses the androids Deckard hunts. (William Sanderson's J.F. Sebastian effectively replaces him in the film.) These are just some world-building details from Dick's work that Blade Runner couldn't fit into a feature-length film.

However, one of these missing elements just made its way into the Blade Runner 2099 TV series.

In Blade Runner 2099's sixth episode, replicants Julius (Tom Burke) and Clotilde (Amy Lennox) drive past a large billboard that advertises "the power of Mercer." The display is a reference to the fictional religion of Mercerism, built around the martyr Wilbur Mercer. Much of the rest of the episode takes place at the abandoned island Mercer Monastery where Cora (Hunter Schafer) grew up.

Mercerism was initially conceptualized in Dick's 1964 short story "The Little Black Box." Followers connect with Mercer by gripping the handles of an empathy box. This device allows the user to experience Mercer's climb to his death: a slow ascent up a hill during which he's stoned repeatedly.

Dick revisits Mercerism in Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, in which Deckard uses an empathy box and sees visions of Mercer. However, radio host Buster Friendly exposes that the Mercer seen in the empathy boxes is simply a character played by an actor. Buster is omitted from Blade Runner and its sequel Blade Runner 2049. In Blade Runner 2099, however, he is played by Hugo Hamlet, and can be spotted in TV broadcasts.

Mercer plays a key role in Blade Runner 2099 episode 6, which is named "Kill the Killers" after Mercer's major tenet: "You shall kill only the killers."

When Cora and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) investigate the monastery,  they encounter the lone Mercerite (David Dencik) living there. He's keeping up a religious telecast devoted to Mercer, and he claims the signal is strong enough to reach Los Angeles. But given that no one else has joined him, it appears his efforts are just shouting into the void.

The Mercerite has an empathy box, and he prompts Olwen to use it while he holds her at gunpoint. Within, she sees Mercer (Tomas Rydval) making his last climb. As unseen forces pelt him with rocks, the empathy box shocks Olwen's hands to mimic the painful experience.

Olwen eventually uses a loose handle from the box to stab her captor. Then, she and Cora escape the island without becoming Mercer converts. (Sorry, Wilbur.)

The episode functions both as a tribute to this piece of world-building and as a key subplot that was initially lost when Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? leaped from page to screen.

Buster Friendly and Wilbur Mercer may not have gotten their time to shine in Blade Runner or Blade Runner 2049, but in a TV series like Blade Runner 2099, there is space to expand on the world and give them a moment in the spotlight, no matter how brief.

#295. The 36 Best Gifts for Dads (2026)

It occurs to me that, as a new(ish) father, and someone who reviews products for a living, I am a nightmare to get gifts for. I’m not alone. Most of my friends have no idea what to get their dad, and end up brainstorming in group chats with anyone they can get their hands on.

Fear not, I’m here to make gifting a little easier this year (or at the very least, contribute to the brainstorm). Below are some of the best WIRED-tested gifts for the dad or father figure in your life, including travel gadgets, dad-approved apparel, and best-in-class earbuds. I’ve personally gifted a few of these to my dad, with great results.

Updated November 2026: I swapped and added a few new picks, including watches and apparel.

Another classic gift I’ve seen win over not just Dad, but everyone else in the room, too (everyone wanted a turn). This massage gun has the signature Theragun triangle grip, which makes it far easier to target hard-to-reach places compared to other brands that have a straight grip. It comes with three ball head attachments (standard, dampener, and thumb), and lasts up to 120 minutes on a single charge.

These are my favorite open ear headphones for anyone, not just Dad. Because they leave your ears open, you can easily hear the world around you, along with your music. That’s why I love them for outdoor runs and bike rides. This premium model uses a mix of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that’s clearer than most smaller open earbuds. You can learn more in our full Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 review.

This Garmin watch is just right for the dad who is getting really into running and wants to dig into more advanced metrics and detailed training plans than what’s offered on most smartwatches. Like any good fitness tracker, the Forerunner 165 has superb battery life (up to 11 days), a colorful touchscreen, and plenty of buttons that make it easy to control with gloved or sweaty hands. It’s also one of the brand’s most affordable running watches. You can learn more in our full Garmin Forerunner 165 review.

I can’t think of many dads who don’t love an electric bike. The Letric XP4 750 isn’t just one of WIRED’s top electric bike picks, it’s one of the best-selling electric vehicles in America, ranking third behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3 in 2024. WIRED reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani says it only took 20 minutes to assemble and lasted well over 50 miles of riding on a single charge. This version has an upgraded 750-watt motor that helps tackle hillier terrain than the original.

This is my favorite power bank, full stop. If I am traveling, going abroad, camping, or just headed to work, I take this power bank. It’s the built-in, retractable USB-C cord that does it for me—it’s there when you need it, and out of the way when you don’t. It’s small enough to pack in any bag and light enough that I barely notice it. Plus, it has an extra USB-A and USB-C port built in, so you can charge multiple devices at once if you want.

I’ve lost count of how many times my Apple AirTag Bluetooth tracker has saved me from the hassle of looking for something. Keys: located. Luggage: tracked. Backpack: safe and sound. Sure, it’s not the most exciting gift in the world, but it’s the epitome of useful and practical. As long as they use an iPhone, that is.

“If you told me I could only have one bag in my life, the 26L version of the GoRuck GR1 would be my pick,” says WIRED operations manager and outdoor expert Scott Gilbertson (he’s also a dad). It’s absolutely in buy-it-for-life territory, built with ultra-durable, water-resistant 1000D Cordura and tested by US Army Special Forces. It’s technically made for rucking, but it can do basically anything you throw at it, travel included. This Huckberry version omits the exterior MOLLE webbing, giving it a sleeker look. You can read more in Gilbertson’s full GoRuck GR1 review.

The best aluminum carry-on suitcase. Aluminum luggage is sleek and durable, with a shell that just looks better with little dents and dings (unlike polycarbonate luggage). Aluminum itself is recyclable and repairable, and the clamps that hold the Rimowa together won’t fail or break as easily as your typical zipper. Rimowa is obviously the “it” brand for this type of luggage, but you can get similar options from Away and Level8 for well under half the price.

A reusable water bottle is something I thought I only needed one of. Turns out, the more the merrier. I now have four and have realized there’s a good place for each one (in my case, one for the house, one for my work bag, and one for the nightstand). The Owala FreeSip has been my favorite for years, usurping my Hydro Flask and S’well for water bottle supremacy. Plus it comes in literally dozens of colors—there’s definitely one he’ll love.

I’ve become a camera person since becoming a dad, with a growing collection that’s frankly getting a little out of hand. Camp Snap is part of that camera pile. It’s one of the simplest ways to take pictures without getting distracted by your phone or overwhelmed by mirrorless camera settings to fiddle with. This latest model adds desperately needed updates like a button to toggle between filters and a faster shutter button. It also comes in a bunch of fun colors, including a few transparent options that remind me of my old Game Boy Color.

If Dad loves to host large get-togethers, parties, or tailgates, this portable party speaker is one of the loudest, most durable I’ve tested. It’s got a clean, understated, loudspeaker-slash-rock-concert look that’s a far cry from the light-show techno vibes of most portable party speakers. It’s very durable, with large silicone balls on each corner for impact protection. Plus, it has a swappable battery. I honestly wouldn’t be surprised if it outlasts most other speakers in his collection. You can learn more in my full Soundboks Rider review.

If he owns an iPhone, chances are he would appreciate an upgraded pair of wireless earbuds. I’ve been testing the newest Apple AirPods 5 for a few weeks now, and I’ve been truly impressed with how good the noise-canceling is, especially for earbuds without eartips. The version I linked above also has improved battery life, a wireless charging case, and volume-swipe controls on each earbud stem.

The classic business traveler over-ear headphones. I’ve been testing these latest Bose for nearly a month now, and they are some of the most comfortable over-ear headphones you can get, with dang good noise-canceling too. If Dad loves his music, podcasts, and TV shows, no matter where he is, these will be a trusty companion for his next adventure, whether that’s on the couch or on his next long-haul flight.

Teenage Engineering needs little introduction—the Swedish company makes some of the nicest-looking, nicest-feeling gadgets that are the envy of basically everyone who doesn’t own one. This is one of the brand's portable samplers, sequencers, and composers that Dad can make music on, wherever he is. Despite its small size, it has ample pads and dials, a built-in microphone and line input for audio recording, 64GB of internal memory, and 999 sample slots.

My vinyl era started long before I became a dad, but it’s only since then that I started caring about how a turntable looks. This one from Flaunce is a minimal faux wood model that looks elegant on a shelf or table, but lets the vinyl take center stage. It has an upgradable cartridge and a built-in phono preamp—Dad just needs to plug it into some powered bookshelf speakers, and voilà.

I basically lived in one of these tees during parental leave. It’s absolutely the softest tee I own, with a fabric that never bothered my sensitive skin. It’s athletic without being too slim-fitting, stretchy without feeling cheap, and a great do-everything (or do nothing on the couch) tee for anyone, not just Dad.

Another do-everything piece of apparel, but decidedly more technical than the Vuori tee. These are my go-to pants for walks, hikes, and camping trips. They are very lightweight and have a reasonably athletic fit, water-repellent finish, adjustable drawstring waist, and durable ripstop polyester I’ve yet to poke a hole through.

The gift that never fails. I’ve seen the Brooks Ghost gifted to me, my dad, my father-in-law, and others. No one has ever looked disappointed. These are great running shoes for just about anyone, with neutral support and plenty of cushion. I’ve used the 18s (and previous 17s, 16s, 15s) for dozens of miles of walking and running this year—they are comfortable and reliable. Plus, you are supposed to replace your running shoes every six months or so, which I’m sure your dad has not done.

Dads who run need more running shirts. I certainly do. This Ten Thousand Session Shirt is one of my go-tos because it is breathable enough for a serious run, but looks normal enough to go to the café afterward. It’s made from 100 percent polyester—no nylon or spandex to be found here, which means it dries fast and absorbs very little water, in my experience.

Sneakers in the office are going extinct—haven’t you heard? WIRED commerce director Cooper Fleishman noticed these on GQ editor Jordan Bowman, and we have to pass along the loafer recommendation because the “buttery smooth” leather alone is worth a small splurge.

The best merino wool socks, period. They are antimicrobial and wick sweat, but also keep your feet dry and keep them thermoregulated. Plus the brand has a lifetime warranty on these socks—if you ever get a hole, send them back for a replacement pair (we did).

This Benrus diver is the rare tool watch you can dress up, thanks to its elegant size and vintage style. It's 20 percent off right now; WIRED commerce director Cooper Fleishman ordered one to test out in December.

…Or spend one tenth the cost of the Benrus for an indestructible Dad watch. Inspired by the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak, this Casio shows great design and good taste doesn't need to cost thousands.

A headlamp is an infinitely useful outdoor tool—you can use it for camping; yard work (early or late in the day); home maintenance; or, if you’re my dad, grilling after the sun has set. I’ve loved using this Biolite headlamp in 2026. It’s bright, comfortable, and has multiple modes, including a focused beam mode, wide floodlight mode, and red-light mode that I’ve loved for bikepacking. Plus it’s USB-C rechargeable—no more rummaging through the battery drawer for AAs.

This premium cooler is the gift that will last them for years and years. It’s made with double-walled vacuum insulation, just like a travel mug. In practice, that means it can keep things cool with less than half as much ice as a regular cooler, and has much thinner walls, which makes for a larger interior space. Yes, it’s pricier than a regular cooler, but its premium design, lightweight body, and ultra-efficient cooling make it a winner for dads everywhere.

I will readily admit I am not a knife guy, but I love this knife. I’m not alone—it’s featured in our Buy It for Life guide, and comes recommended by me, former WIRED senior director Martin Cizmar, and over 2,000 five-star reviews on Amazon. Sure, it’s probably not as bulletproof as that matte-black EDC high-end pocket knife that costs $300, but it’s timeless, classy, and elegant.

If he loves ultralight, this is the cup for him. If he has no idea what ultralight is but wants a super lightweight cup for drinks or snacks around the house, this too is a fun option. Snow Peak is one of our favorite outdoor gear brands, and its lightweight titanium cookware is some of its most popular. I’ve used this cup on bikepacking trips and for snacking around the house alike.

I didn’t think I needed a tiny portable vacuum (I have a perfectly good cordless vacuum), but I was gifted this tiny Hoto vacuum years ago, and it has been endlessly useful. I use it to clean strollers, keyboards, my desk, you name it. It’s small and portable enough to take anywhere you need a quick clean. I gifted one to my brother-in-law, and he uses it to clean his car constantly—it basically lives in his car’s glove compartment.

An on-board diagnostic scanner plugs into your car’s port and pairs to your phone via Bluetooth so you can read and troubleshoot your car’s error codes. It’s a great way for tinkerers to fix car issues themselves and avoid a time-consuming trip to the shop. Former WIRED director Martin Cizmar recommended this scanner from BlueDriver. It has a lot of powerful features that don’t require any subscription to use (unlike many competitors).

Noco makes some of the best portable jump starters—emphasis on portable. This battery-powered jump starter charges with a regular USB-C cable, and is a must-have for anyone who wants to avoid waiting for a buddy car or waiting for a tow. WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tested all kinds of jump starters on his old Land Cruiser, and recommends this one as the best compact option. Not only can it start your car, it can recharge your phone, just like a regular power bank would.

This is the best pizza oven for the dad who doesn’t have space for a full-sized outdoor one. It’s an indoor electric pizza oven that can fit on a countertop, and can heat to up to 850 degrees Fahrenheit. Like all of the brand’s appliances, it’s easy to use, so it's more fun than work to make that fan-favorite pizza just right.

When my son was born last year, I lost the time to grind and brew, so I found myself stocking my fridge with disappointingly bitter bulk-bottled iced coffee (or spending $7 on a café cold brew). My wife got us a coffee subscription to Cometeer, which flash-freezes freshly ground small-batch coffee and ships them in recyclable pods—just add water, hot or cold, to dial in the strength. You can take the time to mix and match roasters each month or just set your faves and forget it. After six months of testing, I can safely say I haven’t had a bad cup. I miss the aromatics I get and comfort I feel from a truly fresh grind, but each pour feels like a tiny treat, even at 5 am. It’s a whole little moment: My 16-month-old chugs his bottle while I stir up oat milk, ice, and Counter Culture. He’s learning to say “cheers.” I look forward to those early mornings a bit more than I used to. —Cooper Fleishman

If they love a cocktail, this toolkit from Umami Mart elevates the mixing experience to something more refined. Umami Mart is an independently owned small business in Oakland that’s part sake bar, part sake class space, and part online barware store. This kit includes a diamond-cut mixing glass, julep strainer, stainless steel jigger, and stainless steel teardrop barspoon, all made in Japan and sourced by the brand.

The Lego DeLorean Time Machine from the Back to the Future trilogy is the perfect centerpiece for any movie buff, but Great Scott, it’s $200. A better alternative is the version from Lego’s Speed Champions series. It’s much cheaper and easier to build (pick either the original with lightning hook or the “future” upgrade with Mr. Fusion and hover wheels), but it has the same charm and display quality. It comes with Doc Brown and Marty McFly Minifigures, but sadly, it won’t hit 88 miles per hour.

Tossing a Frisbee around is part fun, part an excuse to hang out and talk. It’s a classic dads-and-kids activity that lasts for years, even as interests and hobbies change. Former WIRED director Martin Cizmar says that, over time, the ask to toss the Frisbee around shifts from the kid to the adult. Either way, the Aerobie is one of the best flying discs you can buy.

Perhaps the best water gun ever made, the SpryaFour is a very powerful squirt gun that can shoot accurately from up to 50 feet away. It has a fully digital smart display that lets you select between shooting styles and shows you how much ammo you have left. It refills much faster than the SpyraThree (20 shots in about 12 seconds). It’s recommended for kids (and adults) 14 and up.

#294. Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom.

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.

New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid.

Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.
