#292. Some fans whistle as Lionel Messi's name is announced as Paris Saint-Germain's season hits new low

Paris Saint-Germain’s miserable season went from bad to worse on Sunday as the team suffered a second straight home defeat with a 1-0 loss to Lyon.

Even before the game kicked off, Lionel Messi bore the brunt of the frustrations of some PSG fans who whistled when his name appeared on the big screen during the announcement of the starting lineup.

Lionel Messi passes 100 international goals with hat-trick against Curaçao

After Alexadre Lacazette missed a first-half penalty, Bradley Barcola’s goal 10 minutes into the second period was enough to earn Lyon the three points on a night that PSG rarely looked like threatening the visiting goal.

Lens’ 1-0 victory over Rennes and Marseille’s 1-1 draw with Montepellier means both teams are now just six points behind PSG at the top of Ligue 1, and even the domestic title may slip from the team’s grasp.

The reaction of some fans on Sunday must have felt a world away from the adulation and worship Messi received during his recent return to Argentina for friendlies against Panama and Curaçao as the country continued its World Cup celebrations.

Messi’s arrival at the Parc des Princes was supposed to be the missing piece that would help PSG finally win the Champions League, the trophy the club’s Qatari owners crave the most.

So far, the only major trophy the team has won since Messi joined was Ligue 1 last season, a title – it’s fair to say – PSG would likely have won without him.

Messi has 34 goal contributions in all competitions for PSG this season – 18 goals and 17 assists – second only to Mbappé’s 38 and head coach Christophe Galtier refused to lay the blame for the team’s failures at the Argentine’s feet.

“I found it [the jeering] hard to listen to,” Galtier told reporters, per the Athletic. “There may be expectations for Messi and Mbappe to unlock difficult situations. Messi tries very hard, they didn’t all work out; but around him, the other players also need to do their jobs.”

“We can’t expect everything from Leo and Kylian,” he added.

Lionel Messi mania grips Argentina as World Cup celebrations continue

Up next for PSG is a season-defining week as Galtier’s side travels to a Nice team that is unbeaten in 13 matches, before hosting Lens at the Parc des Princes.

PSG has lost two of its three matches since being dumped out of the Champions League by Bayern Munich last month, and only limped past relegation-threatened Brest with a 90th minute Kylian Mbappé winner.

After his team’s victory, Lyon head coach Laurent Blanc said the Champions League or bust mentality has been detrimental to PSG’s performances.

“Paris’ problem is when the No. 1 objective of the Champions League is no longer accessible, it seems that the season no longer exists – and at all levels,” he told reporters.

#291. How Jump-Roping Toy Soldiers Accidentally Took Over Your FYP

Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”

He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage. And “experts” and “recent polling data,” “fans believe it is Holidave who holds the most whimsy” out of all the SeaWorld toy soldiers.

This is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando. Per toy soldier lore, in addition to Jackary Jingleson there’s also Sugarsnookie, Soulja Toy, Big Chestnut, and Frosty McSleigh. And all of the edits are the same: an AI-generated narrator recites stats about the toy soldiers, such as their net worth and their vertical leap, as if they were elite athletes and not niche theme park performers.

For the past two weeks, fan page videos featuring the jump-roping toy soldiers have been going viral, with @wejumprope_memes’ most popular video garnering 1.2 million views. In the comments sections, fans debate the merits and deficits of each toy soldier, declaring their allegiance to their favorite as if they were a ’90s boy band: “Jackery Jingleson is having a banner year! His speed is incomparable, his style undeniable, and his technique is utterly flawless,” reads one comment. Another disputes this, writing “Soulja Toy the underrated gem.”

Mostly, people seem confused as to why these videos keep showing up in their algorithm and why they keep watching them. “I have a PhD and lecture at a university. And yet here I am,” one commenter writes on a video about whether Major Bounce, a new toy soldier, will show up for the 2026 season. (In a November 20 Reel announcing “major news for the jump-roping toy soldier community,” he finally did.)

As it turns out, there’s a simple explanation for the virality. @wejumprope_memes is run by Devin Meek, an Orlando-based professional entertainer who works for WeFlip, a production company that produces acrobatics shows. But he’s now perhaps best known as his alter ego—Holidave.

What started just a few weeks ago as him making memes to make his coworkers laugh has metamorphosed into an internet sensation, with the toy soldiers amassing a genuine, and ardent, fandom. “I really just made these videos for my friends in the jump-roping community,” Meek tells WIRED. “But I guess they resonated with more people than I thought.”

The videos are piggybacking on a larger—and increasingly absurd—trend of seasonal theme park employees going viral. In September, as WIRED previously reported, SeaWorld Orlando enjoyed a bump in ticket sales thanks to Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-themed Halloween scare zone at SeaWorld Orlando that featured swaggering bad boys from the romantasy genre flirting with guests. And last month, women on TikTok swooned over Archer and Fryboy, two performers at Hersheypark Halloween known for sliding around in kneepads wearing tactical streetwear and clown makeup, a practice known as “sliding.”

Meek, who has been jumping rope for the past 20 years, was inspired to create the videos featuring Sugarsnookie, Jackary, and the like after seeing the success of Archer and Fryboy, who have a combined more than 3.1 million followers on TikTok. “It was such an interesting phenomenon, because I’m somebody who is in a very similar position where I work a few months out of the year as a holiday-themed performer,” he says. “So I got a kick out of it.”

Meek already had an account, @wejumprope_memes, where he posted jump-roping fails and compilations. He posted one video on November 13 featuring old footage from SeaWorld Orlando, where he’s been performing with the other toy soldiers for the past six years. (The group got started during the height of the Covid pandemic—hence, why they wear masks during their shows.) “Fryboy who? Move over, Archer,” it begins, before introducing the lore of Jackery Jingleson, the most “light-hearted, nonchalant” of the toy soldiers.

To Meek’s surprise, the video received almost a million views and 588 comments, most of which were not from fellow members of the jumping community but from total strangers. So Meek posted more toy soldier lore on his meme page, introducing Big Chestnut (“a powerful jumper”), Soulja Toy (the developer of the “Christmas Ice Storm 261”), Sugarsnookie (“the girl’s girl of the group,” who is dating Big Chestnut) and Frosty McSleigh (“he has the fastest salute time of all the toy soldiers.”)

Though the lore is fictional, it’s also based on the jumpers’ actual skills and personalities: the jumpers who play Big Chestnut and Sugarsnookie are actually in a long-term relationship, and Jackery Jingleson, perhaps the most popular of the group, once held the world record for the fastest jump roper in the United States. “Honestly, that makes [the popularity of the memes] even funnier to us,” he says.

Though some fans have speculated in the comments that the toy soldier memes are a marketing campaign for SeaWorld Orlando, Meek denies that’s the case: He doesn’t tag SeaWorld in the comments, nor has he been in contact with the theme park about his page. (SeaWorld Orlando did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

“This is something that is so targeted to people who are internet-brained and have this ironic sense of humor,” he says. “And that’s exactly the type of person who’ll tune out immediately if they feel like they’re being sold something on the internet.”

Others have even speculated that there is an actual feud brewing between the SeaWorld Orlando “jumpers” and the Southern California–based “sliders,” though Meek says the rivalry is playful, and he has even reached out to collab with them. (The sliders may view it differently: So far, he says, they “don’t seem super interested” in joining forces.)

What has surprised Meek the most, however, is that very few commenters suspect that the toy soldiers themselves are behind the memes. In fact, he’s been shocked by how many organic meme fan pages have popped up within the past week, with people drawing their own fan art of Holidave saluting or Jackery Jingleson jumping. WeFlip has also been deluged with business inquiries: “People are like, how can we get Jackery Jingleson out here?”

Essentially, what started as an inside joke within an extremely niche community has evolved into an inside joke for the internet at large. “I think people like the feeling of being in on a joke and being a part of it and building it up,” he says.

So what’s next for the SeaWorld Orlando jump-roping toy soldiers? The rotating cast typically performs at the park on the weekends, ramping up appearances as it gets closer to the holiday season. Meek also shares that the toy soldiers will “likely cross state lines” in the coming months, including a stint at the Christmas market in Cullman, Alabama. Frosty McSleigh, renowned for his 0.08-second salute, plus a slew of new, yet-to-be-introduced toy soldiers will also make an appearance.

Though it may come as a disappointment to some that the roots of the toy soldier phenomenon were inorganic, Meek isn’t concerned. “The people are real. The athleticism is real. The lore is real,” he says. “For all of these people, jump rope is their life, and we’re super-dedicated to teaching it and sharing it. And I think people can feel that.”

Bruce Willis’ wife, Emma Heming Willis, has celebrated their elder daughter’s birthday with a trip down memory lane.

Mabel Willis turned 11 on Sunday, and her proud mom marked the occasion by sharing a montage of family photos and videos taken over the years, set to the song “Pictures Of You” by The Cure.

“Happy 11th Birthday Mabel Ray!” Heming Willis wrote in the caption.

Emma Heming Willis speaks out about finding community as a caregiver: 'This journey can feel very dark'

“Your energy is infectious,” she continued, praising her little girl for the way she “can light a whole room with your smile and warmth.”

“How you love and care for your family and friends is beautiful to witness. Keep shining my love and always remember to #liveitup,” Heming Willis added.

Heming Willis and Willis married in 2009. Along with Mabel, the couple also have an 8-year-old daughter, Evelyn. Willis also has daughters Rumer, Scout and Tallulah with his ex-wife, Demi Moore.

Willis is clearly a doting dad. One picture in Heming Willis’ montage shows the “Die Hard” star holding baby Mabel while planting a kiss on her forehead, while a more recent image shows a beaming Willis hanging out in nature with his preteen.

Bruce Willis sings with his family in birthday tribute video from ex Demi Moore

Heming Willis penned an equally heartfelt tribute last month when her husband celebrated his 68th birthday. Sharing a video montage on Instagram, she referred to the actor as “pure love.”

In February, Willis’ family announced that his speaking disorder, aphasia, had progressed into a form of dementia called frontotemporal dementia, or FTD.

“Today there are no treatments for the disease, a reality that we hope can change in the years ahead,” they said in an update shared online. “As Bruce’s condition advances, we hope that any media attention can be focused on shining a light on this disease that needs far more awareness and research.”

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, FTD refers to “a group of disorders caused by progressive nerve cell loss in the brain’s frontal lobes (the areas behind your forehead) or its temporal lobes.” These areas of the brain are generally associated with personality, behavior and language.

#287. 'I've lost her forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract

For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or exposes them.

When does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.

For more than 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.

The same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.

But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.

Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.

The reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.

They're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.

"It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich said. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry."

"Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she said.

The new AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.

Fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.

Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.

If an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.

"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the company to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.

"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," said Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes."

He would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.

Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.

"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.

Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon elephant Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.

"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies."

He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.

According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.

The suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.

For Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?"

Netflix said it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.

For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.

Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.

"Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.

Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.

"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," said Fröhlich.

But if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again."

#286. AI is straining America’s open records systems

Startups are mining public data for AI products, while citizens use chatbots to file more requests.

In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”

As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”

Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

#285. Thanksgiving parade 2026: Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade start time, streaming options, weather concerns

Thanksgiving is almost here, and for some folks, the most important part of the holiday isn't the food, family, or football. It's watching a bunch of big floats during a parade in New York City.

OK, maybe that's not literally true, but the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an annual touchstone for lots of folks, and it's almost here. As always, there are lots of things to know about it, such as when it starts, where you can watch it, and, this year especially, whether the weather will play a role in the parade playing out as expected. Let's get into it.

First and foremost, the parade starts at 8:30 a.m. ET and runs until noon on Thursday. It's worth noting that, unlike most other live televised events, it will not air simultaneously in every time zone. Instead, per NBC News, it will air from 8:30 to around noon in each time zone, so no matter where you are, turn the TV on at 8:30.

There will also be an encore at 2 p.m., in case football isn't your cup of tea.

The parade will air on NBC, so if you have a TV that gets local channels via cable, an antenna, or another way to watch TV, just turn on NBC. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

If you don't have any of those things, Peacock will work, too. I should note that you'll need at least Peacock Premium to stream your local NBC station, and there is no free trial for that. You'll either have to pay $12.99 per month or borrow someone else's login.

According to NBC News, this year's parade will feature 100 inflatables in total, the most they've ever used for one of these. You can see the full balloon lineup on the Macy's website, but rest assured that all your favorites are likely included, like Sonic the Hedgehog and the Pink Panther. There are also new ones, like a DoorDash float and a GEICO float. One float will also act as a tribute of sorts for Fiona the hippo, which is nice.

Performers include Teddy Swims and Megan Moroney on the main stage, with other floats featuring acts such as the Baha Men, Blues Traveler, Icona Pop, and Devo. There's a little something for everyone.

And now for the potentially bad news: There's a weather system moving its way up the East Coast that threatens to disrupt the parade, per NBC News.

Two storms combined into one in the American South, with the result expected to bring wind gusts of up to 45mph to New York City starting on Thursday morning. This is a problem because the city has an upper limit of 34mph for gusts regarding big inflatable objects. So far, it appears the parade is scheduled to happen as planned, but keep your head on a swivel and maybe have a plan B for family entertainment on Thursday morning in case there are problems.

#283. The Download: AI swamping open records, and firefighting for permafrost

Plus: Hackers reportedly used an AI tool to breach US spy agencies.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

AI has intensified investors' interest in public records. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered "signals" that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent.

Find out how AI is testing the limits of America's right to know.

In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and soil insulating the permafrost below. Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.

Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

—Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel skewers Jensen Huang's swift reinstatement as Nvidia's CEO.

Teaching a computer to use human language requires an inhuman amount of data. An LLM can easily churn through a hundred thousand times more words than a person will experience in the process of mastering their mother tongue.

This yawning divide between children and machines is called the data efficiency gap. It raises a tantalizing question for researchers: How can children learn so much with so little?

By reverse-engineering how they learn, scientists hope to create more efficient AI models—and perhaps settle enduring questions about language and children's developing minds. Here’s how they’re trying to close the data gap.

Early Black Friday deals started rolling in weeks ago, but now we're well into the official sales. Yes, instead of standing in a cold line at 4 a.m. the day after Thanksgiving, we get to shop online under cozy blankets while watching Christmas movies.

This year, Black Friday falls on Nov. 27, but that date isn't all that important these days. Almost every major retailers has already started official Black Friday sales. We expect to see some special deals drop on Nov. 27, but if you're looking to shop Black Friday sales, it's your time to shine.

Absolutely yes. The mega-retailer's sale kicked off Thursday, Nov. 19 — more info on the full date range of the sale is below. Expect deals on everything from the year's top tech to home essentials. Considering prices went up this year on pretty much Apple devices except for AirPods, Black Friday will be the time to pick up new Apple devices. #280. How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

Rising electricity demand is locking in fossil-fuel generation.

In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report. That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

#279. Data center emissions are worse than we knew, Harvard study confirms

This past election, Americans across the country rejected data centers, voting to restrict new projects in their communities. As voters push back against data centers, a new study out of Harvard reveals startling revelations about the severity of the pollution they create.

Pollution from data centers is three times higher than previously estimated, according to a new study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

The study examined 403 "hyperscale" data centers and found that emissions from these facilities were underestimated. In fact, the lead author Gianluca Guidi believes that their research only provides a "floor estimate." When factoring in the thousands of data centers across the country, many of which were not included in the study, the energy use is likely much higher.

The study found that the largest data centers in the U.S. use as much energy in a single year as the state of Michigan does. Carbon emissions from these data centers surpassed those of entire countries.

Researchers found that 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. during the study period came from data centers. A single data center included in the study consumed as much energy as 30,000 homes on average. #278. German police respond to multiple school bomb threats

Police in Germany are responding to bomb threats against a series of schools, but say that at present they don't believe them to be credible. Danish authorities are reporting a similar series of apparent hoaxes.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.

"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release. "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages."

Police said they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.

"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they said.

Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also said they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.

Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."

This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Italy earlier in the month.

It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.

#277. Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out the New York Times

Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

Twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk says too bad

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

Although the New York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was quickly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual users would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent users such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

By muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile users. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”

“There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he said in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also said that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in users’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

#276. The Iowa Lead Detonation Happened. Now the Real Work Begins to Study It

On Wednesday morning, the US Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide outside of Middletown, Iowa.

Environmental Protection Administration chief Lee Zeldin told CNN shortly after the explosion that preliminary monitoring from the site detected no lead in the air around the site.

But the full extent of the fallout may not be certain for at least a few days. A barrage of government, university, and citizen monitoring and testing projects are underway. Air, soil, and water samples they’ve collected will determine the extent of lead exposure, if any, in Middletown and the surrounding area.

The lead azide has been on the base near Middletown for decades, but recently the Army deemed it unstable and too dangerous to move and remediate. Poor communication between the Army and towns in the path of the fallout led to a public uproar. While the federal government stepped up its mitigation measures—the Army dug a dam around the detonation site, while NASA stepped in with research jets and satellites for monitoring—universities had already been swinging into action due to the chaotic rollout.

Several departments at the University of Iowa kicked into gear to begin to set up air and soil monitoring stations late last week. “Initially we did not know that [the] EPA or Army or anybody else was going to be doing anything,” says Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the university.

Scientists at Purdue University, nearly 300 miles away, also put out a call for soil samples from Middletown.

“We learned about the detonation late last week; once we learned of the initial delay in detonation date we decided to put forth the call,” says Ellen Wells, a professor of public health at Purdue who is helping lead the testing.

Surrounding towns were notified in late October that the Army wanted to conduct pre- and post-detonation soil sampling for “an intentional, controlled detonation” of a “quantity of lead azide”—seemingly the only notification that many towns in the initial modeled path of the fallout say they received before a press release issued by the Army days before the planned explosion.

The lack of communication has, understandably, instilled a lot of public distrust in the federal government, including agencies’ monitoring programs. Thorne says that efforts like the University of Iowa’s are not meant to displace federal monitoring, but rather to supplement and support it—and hopefully reassure the public.

“We and the EPA are doing similar exposure assessment efforts. If they agree, they can give us some confidence,” he says. “For people who might be concerned about the veracity of what the government tells them, if their findings are in alignment with ours, then I think that helps quell some of those concerns.”

Thorne says that the soil samples the University of Iowa scientists had measured before the detonation had low levels of lead. “If I saw something like a 10 fold increase in the amount of lead in the soil 20 miles downwind, I’d be concerned with that,” he says.

Some soil testing can be done instantaneously with devices that can image the soil’s surface, using a gun device that fires X-ray beams into a sample and measures the specific electromagnetic signature of lead atoms that bounce back. While Wells and her team don’t have those instruments in the field, they are planning on using them to analyze the samples they receive. More sensitive lab equipment can provide even more granular data, though Thorne estimates those results could take about a week.

In addition to monitoring being done by the Army and the EPA, which is maintaining a live website of air quality results, University of Iowa scientists are monitoring the plume to figure out where the highest concentration of lead may settle. They’re also collecting data on particulate matter in the air around the detonation site for analysis, sending air filters to the lab for more detailed results.

“As these data are compiled over the holiday week to the early next week, I think we'll start to have a bigger picture of roughly how much loading we have of the soil at various places downwind and what we can expect from that,” says Thorne.

A lot of concern online has centered around how additional lead in the soil may impact crops in Iowa, one of the central agricultural hubs for soybeans and corn. Jeffrey Catalano, a professor of earth and environmental sciences at Washington University in Saint Louis, says that there’s a large amount of research showing that plants like corn are actually pretty bad at absorbing lead.

“The hazard is more like, if soil with lead in it gets stuck to leaves, and you eat leaves that have lead-rich soil on them,” he says. “If you take some corn crops next year versus this year and measure their lead content, I don’t think you would see anything other than random variations. I’m not worried about food produced in Iowa.”

Municipal drinking water is also unlikely to be affected because most treatment plants are designed to remove lead from water supplies, says Patrick McNamara, a professor of environmental engineering at Marquette University. It’s more worrisome for private wells or streams on people’s property where livestock may drink. McNamara suggests that owners use at-home lead water tests for safety.

While the detonation and haphazard announcements leading up to it raised alarm bells, both Thorne and Catalano say that there are communities dealing with legacy pollution around the country that are exposed to dangerous levels of lead every day that deserve attention—and remediation.

“I've done work in places like East Chicago, Indiana, where they built a housing project and a school on the grounds of a former lead smelting plant—we were seeing soil lead levels that are roughly 10,000-fold higher than what we've measured in Iowa this week,” Thorne says. “There are a lot of places around the country where there's a much greater lead hazard than I'm going to anticipate what we’ll end up with here. I don't want to over-sell this one when we recognize that there are places where people are really suffering, and need to be remediated for the health of their children.”

#275. Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real

Technical details are still limited, but we already know it’s fun to drive.

It wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

That’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that’s usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

So, for the company’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance.

That EV battery layout, stacked behind the two-seat cabin rather than sandwiched below it, isn’t novel. It’s the same setup that Tesla used on the original Roadster back in 2008. Back then it was done for cost reasons as much as anything, enabling Tesla to repurpose a Lotus chassis meant to hold an internal combustion engine in the middle.

For Porsche’s new Boxster (and the Audi Concept C, which is built on the same platform), that pack enables the low seating position and also delivers a rearward weight bias (40:60 front/rear) that’s in keeping with the last-generation 718 Boxster, the internal combustion model killed by EU cybersecurity regulations last year.

Porsche isn’t saying how big the new roadster’s battery is in terms of charge capacity, only that its size was chosen to balance range and weight. We also don’t have an idea of rated range, charging speed, nor battery composition, but I can say the battery pack is based on an 800 V architecture like the electric Macan, so hopefully we can expect charging performance that at least matches that SUV’s 270 kW.

The new Boxster also shares a motor with the Macan. Porsche is not quoting any specs yet, but it puts out about 500 hp (370 kW) to the rear wheels on the Macan Turbo. You can place your bets on whether the Boxster application will result in more or less power. I would take the over, but regardless, it’s enough to sprint this electric roadster to 62 mph (100 km/h) in under 3.0 seconds, making it the quickest Boxster ever.

But it’s also the largest and heaviest. I was told the new Boxster’s curb weight will be somewhere in the ballpark of a current-generation 911, so in the region of 3,300 to 3,700 pounds (roughly 1,500 to 1,700 kg), meaning it has gained at least a few hundred pounds. That’s light for an EV but heavy for a roadster. Its wheelbase has grown accordingly.

You can absolutely feel that on the road. The 718 just doesn’t have the same buzzy eagerness as the latest 718 Boxster or Cayman. But that doesn’t mean it’s less fun to drive. In fact, I think most people would say it’s much more fun. Nearly doubling the old car’s base power output will do that.

This car, though, is about a lot more than acceleration. It still turns and handles incredibly well, borrowing much of its suspension, steering, and even chassis from the current-generation 911. Few would call a 911 a boring car, and the 718 is a step more aggressive even than that coupe.

That’s in part thanks to the response afforded by the electric powertrain, which isn’t saddled by the lazy throttle application caused by turbochargers and modern emission regulations. It’s sharper even than the latest 911 GTS, which required a trick electrically assisted turbocharger plus a battery and electric motor to bring the EV feel to a car driven by internal combustion.

To bring some of the charm of internal combustion to an EV, Porsche followed in the footsteps of the Hyundai Ioniq 5N by adding synthesized shifting and engine noises to the mix. Many cringe at the thought of an EV wailing unnecessarily, but having driven many battery-powered machines that make gas-powered noises, I can say with assurance that they always dial up the fun factor.

What they often lack is authenticity. Porsche sampled the sound of what its engineers determined was the sweetest-sounding 718: the 981-generation Boxster GTS. The new 718 Boxster replicates both that car’s 3.4 L flat-six and its seven-speed dual-clutch transmission, controlled by the paddles behind the steering wheel.

Enable the system, which Porsche calls E-Shift, then put the Boxster into launch control, and you’re in for a bit of a show: The car not only sounds like it’s bouncing off of a rev limiter, but the car itself actually shakes. It does this by pulsing the electric motor, vibrating in much the same way that the original Harley-Davidson Livewire did.

Lift off the brake and the Boxster blasts forward, again doing the sprint to 60 in less than 3 seconds. All the while, the pretend engine is screaming and running through its mock gears, either automatically or at your command with the paddles. In manual mode, the car will hit that artificial rev limiter and abruptly stop accelerating, so you’d better be quick to grab that next gear.

This whole system is there to add a greater sense of emotion to the car, but it does serve a practical purpose. Slinging the 718 around the tight, twisty circuit at the Los Angeles Porsche Experience Center, I was better able to judge my speed through corners by listening to the pretend engine that sounded all the world like it was spinning happily behind my head.

Don’t like it? Press the blue button on the steering wheel and it all goes away, but I have a feeling most people will want it on, at least when they’re driving for fun. They will certainly want it on when cruising into their local Cars & Coffee, since you can hear the sound outside the car as well as on the inside.

Cruising is better in the new 718 than the older model as well. Its adaptive suspension, dialed down to Normal mode, handles concrete separation joints on the highway and bumpy roads without issue.

And it offers something extremely rare on the EV scene: true drop-top motoring. The top folds itself down in somewhere around 10 seconds, tucking itself neatly on top of that battery pack. It also offers reasonable practicality, with a frunk in the nose plus a decently wide if shallow trunk out back. Both are roughly big enough to handle a carry-on suitcase or a couple of backpacks. That’s about it, though. There’s effectively no room behind the seats.

So, from a lifestyle perspective, it’s a bit more flexible and a bit more comfortable than the previous-generation Boxster, and from a power and aggression standpoint, it’s on another planet. Still, there’s no hiding that increase in weight and wheelbase. This truly feels like a cross-breed between a Boxster and a Carrera, which will disappoint some purists, but if you had to pick a pair of parents for a new model, you could do a lot worse than those two.

#272. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

From such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”

#271. COP deadlock prompts calls for a reset of climate diplomacy

COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a final agreement, divided over a reference to "fossil fuels." But was the decision to walk away from a watered-down text actually a show of strength?

The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.

After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact."

"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," said Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.

One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.

Around 130 parties — among them vulnerable island nations, developing countries and richer EU members — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text, to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.

The deadlock signals a failure for the UN process. But the number of countries willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength, and one that had been long coming.

The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared three years ago in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner." But it has been omitted from every text since.

Yet this year's climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists said would safeguard the world from the worst impacts of planetary heating.

And so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.

"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity and the law," said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law.

"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good."

The lack of agreement was not solely about fossil fuels; money also played a part.

Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.

Countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events. Catastrophes like flooding, drought and wildfires have been fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Often the worst hit are poorer countries with low rates of greenhouse gas emissions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.

With the United States  — the world's biggest historical emitter  — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers accusing the EU of hypocrisy.

"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, said in a statement.

As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.

The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.

Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted — it made up part of the rejected final agreement — more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.

It's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum, driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.

There has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. The present model, based on consensus, requires all countries to agree on every measure. There have been many calls for majority-rule decision making, which might have forced the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.

But ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and quickly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.

"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," said UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.
